Reading

The innocent reading first. Three common words are read as a topic, the topic is surveyed, and the organisation of that name is placed within it, from its own page and the research the topic has drawn.

Findings
  • THE TOPIC FOR THE NETWORK. The record is the network at aiandfaith.org. The composition opens on the topic; the network is the first bullet of the third section, and its home page the first card.
  • THE NETWORK, WHERE IT IS REACHED, HELD. 'A global nonprofit network of faith leaders, technologists, ethicists, and scholars'. The record: 'a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators, and partner organizations'. Its five pillars and its menu of traditions are absent; 'nonprofit' comes from the LinkedIn card. Checked 2026-10-31 against the Revelation First census record of 2026-10-30 and the sources it saved.
  • A MEASUREMENT, FROM ELSEWHERE. The record's negative tag keeps the network apart from a measurement of AI systems; the composition supplies one: the Consortium for Evaluating Faith and Ethics in AI found that 'general-purpose LLMs systematically omit or gloss over faith and religious context when handling everyday ethical dilemmas' (the BYU News card: 'announced May 2026', '14 LLMs'). The page names the body 'The Consortium for Evaluation of Faith and Ethics in AI (CEFE-AI)', and the words 'systematically omit or gloss over' are the composition's. It is the field's own question, asked by another body.
  • FIGURES BEYOND THE RECORD. The Barna percentages are the Barna card's. The claim that 'Major tech companies (including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft) have actively engaged with religious leaders' is on no readable card: the Axios page refused the fetch, and the nearest is the title of the Firstpost video.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

An organisation named for its subject is composed as its subject. What is useful for the field is what the composition brings in from outside the record: a consortium that measures how AI answers treat religion, which the census's pending list does not yet hold.

Supplied as an attached file.] [QUERENT] AI and Faith [SYSTEM] The intersection of artificial intelligence and faith spans ethics, spiritual authority, and technological governance. The Trust and Authority Shift • Growing Reliance on AI: Research from organizations like Barna Group shows that many practicing Christians increasingly turn to AI tools for personal domains, including financial stability (61%), general well-being (56%), self-understanding (54%), relationships (53%), and spiritual growth (48%). • The Spiritual Authority Gap: Roughly 30% to 44% of younger demographics (such as Gen Z and Millennials) feel AI guidance can match that of human pastors, though pastors themselves express low trust (6%–12%) in AI as a spiritual authority. • Core Anxieties: Practicing Christians cite major concerns regarding scriptural misinterpretation (83%), pastor replacement (72%), replacing God (65%), and losing faith (73%). Tech Companies Turning to Faith for Ethics • Moral Alignment Initiatives: Major tech companies (including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft) have actively engaged with religious leaders, scholars, and ethicists from over 15 religious traditions to help inform AI morality and alignment. • The Consensus Challenge: Studies from the Consortium for Evaluating Faith and Ethics in AI (CEFE-AI)—including a multi-institution consortium involving BYU, Notre Dame, Baylor, and Yeshiva—reveal that general-purpose LLMs systematically omit or gloss over faith and religious context when handling everyday ethical dilemmas (such as grief, marriage, guilt, and depression), while sometimes exhibiting measurable biases toward or against specific traditions. • Theologians' Critique: Scholars like Noreen Herzfeld note that AI models are not sentient, lack an embodied existence or a soul, and caution against "religion washing" or reducing human identity down to biological algorithms. Collaborative and Pluralist Frameworks • AI and Faith: A global nonprofit network of faith leaders, technologists, ethicists, and scholars works to apply ancient religious wisdom to modern AI governance, human dignity, and responsible innovation. • Interfaith and Academic Dialogues: Programs like Harvard’s
